title: Shopping
goal: Shop on your own in Norway: state quantities, ask prices, and use *noen* and *noe* — two little words that English splits across "some" and "any".
bekal: name measures: *en liter*, *et kilo*, *ei flaske*, *en pose*
ask the price, pay, and turn down a plastic bag
wave: Review **unit 12** first: cover the Norwegian, look at the English, and rebuild the dialogue. Say the five forms of *liten* once more.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — På butikken
dialogs.intro: A small corner supermarket, Saturday morning. Budi has been standing in front of the milk shelf too long, and Ingrid finally finds him there.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Hva gjør du? Du har stått her i fem minutter.
lines.id: What are you doing? You've been standing here for five minutes.
lines.literal: what do you? you have stood here in five minutes.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Det står ti slags melk her. Hvilken skal jeg ta?
lines.id: There are ten kinds of milk here. Which one should I take?
lines.literal: it stands ten kinds milk here. which shall I take?

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Ta lettmelk. Én liter holder ei uke.
lines.id: Take the low-fat milk. One liter lasts a week.
lines.literal: take light-milk. one liter holds a week.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Og brød? Jeg trenger noe til frokost.
lines.id: And bread? I need something for breakfast.
lines.literal: and bread? I need something for breakfast.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Ta et grovbrød. Har du noen egg hjemme?
lines.id: Take a whole-grain loaf. Do you have any eggs at home?
lines.literal: take a coarse-bread. have you some eggs at-home?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nei, ingen. Og ingen ost heller.
lines.id: No, none. And no cheese either.
lines.literal: no, none. and no cheese either.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Da tar vi tolv egg og et halvt kilo brunost.
lines.id: Then let's get twelve eggs and half a kilo of *brunost*.
lines.literal: then take we twelve eggs and a half kilo brown-cheese.

lines.speaker: Ingrid:
lines.text: Brun og søt. Du kommer til å hate den eller elske den.
lines.id: Brown and sweet. You'll either hate it or love it.
lines.literal: brown and sweet. you come to hate it or love it.

lines.speaker: Kassereren:
lines.text: Det blir tre hundre og førtiåtte kroner. Trenger du pose?
lines.id: That's 348 kroner. Do you need a bag?
lines.literal: it becomes three hundred and forty-eight kroner. need you bag?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nei takk, jeg har med meg egen.
lines.id: No thanks, I brought my own.
lines.literal: no thanks, I have with me self.

lines.speaker: Kassereren:
lines.text: Fint. Vær så god, og god helg.
lines.id: Great. Here you go, and have a good weekend.
lines.literal: fine. be so good, and good weekend.

notes: **The measure goes straight before the item, with no linking word.** *En liter melk*, *et kilo poteter*, *ei flaske vann*, *en kopp kaffe*. English inserts *of* (*a liter **of** milk*); Norwegian doesn't. Leave the *of* out.

**Noen versus noe** is a distinction you have to set up on purpose. *Noen* is for countable things (*noen egg* — some eggs), *noe* for uncountable things (*noe brød* — some bread). English uses "some" for both, so the split feels new.
**Ingen and ingenting** are the negative partners. *Ingen egg* (no eggs), *ingenting* (nothing). Since both are already negative, **don't add *ikke***.

**Det står ti slags melk** uses *å stå* for things standing on a shelf. Norwegian pays close attention to how things are positioned: *å stå* (stand), *å ligge* (lie), *å henge* (hang), *å sitte* (sit). Using *å være* for all of them isn't wrong, but it sounds less precise.
**Et halvt kilo** — notice *halvt* takes the *et*-word form because *kilo* is an *et*-word. *Halv* follows the ordinary adjective rules from unit 12.
**Du kommer til å hate den** is one way to talk about the future; it means "you're going to" with a predicting tone. The full future forms come in unit 17.

grammars.title: Quantities and measures
body: Uncountable things need a container or measure in front. Notice that the noun stands **bare** — no *en/ei/et* and no ending.
after: ⚠️ Don't insert *av*. *Ei flaske av vann* is wrong — just *ei flaske vann*. This habit comes from English and is heard immediately.
When there's more than one, the measure goes plural, not the item: *to flasker vann*, *tre kopper kaffe*, *fire stykker kake*.
To ask: *hvor mye melk?* (uncountable) and *hvor mange egg?* (countable) — just like "how much" and "how many".

grammars.title: Noen, noe, ingen, ingenting
body: Four little words that complete each other. This table shows the whole system at once.
after: *Noen* also means "someone": *Er det noen hjemme?* (Is anyone home?). One word, two jobs — the context decides.
⚠️ *Ingen* and *ingenting* **are already negative**. *Jeg har ikke ingen egg* is wrong twice over. The right forms are *jeg har ingen egg* or *jeg har ikke noen egg*.
In longer sentences with a helping verb, Norwegian prefers *ikke noe* to *ingenting*: *Jeg har ikke sett noe* is more natural than *jeg har sett ingenting*.

grammars.title: Phrases you'll need at the checkout
body: Learn these as whole blocks. At the checkout there's no time to build sentences from scratch.

head: Norsk
English
rows: Do you need a bag? — No thanks.
Do you have a loyalty card?

after: *Trumf* is the points program of Norway's biggest supermarket chain, and you'll get the question at almost every checkout. The standard answer if you don't have one: *nei, det har jeg ikke*.
Prices in Norway include tax — the number on the shelf is what you pay. Nothing is added at the checkout, and there's no tipping in shops.

blocks.text: Notice that *kjøtt* is pronounced **hyöt** and *kylling* **HYÜL-ling** — *kj-* and *k-* before *y* both make a soft hiss. And *ost* is pronounced **oost**, one more *o* that sounds like "oo".
Many food words are **uncountable** and stand without *en/ei/et*: *melk*, *ost*, *smør*, *kjøtt*, *ris*, *sukker*, *salt*. To give an amount, use a measure from the earlier table.

items: **Shops close earlier than you'd think** — usually at 9 or 10 p.m. on weekdays, 6 or 8 p.m. on Saturdays. On Sundays **almost every shop is closed**; only small corner stores called *nærbutikk* and gas stations are open.

**Alcohol is sold separately.** Beer can be bought in supermarkets until 8 p.m. (Saturdays until 6 p.m.), while wine and spirits are sold only in the state-run stores called **Vinmonopolet**, which have even shorter hours.

**Bottles and cans are returned.** Every plastic bottle and can carries a *pant* (deposit) of 2–3 kroner, which you get back from a machine at the shop entrance. Collecting them isn't embarrassing; everyone does it.
**Plastic bags cost money**, and almost everyone brings their own cloth bag.
**Food prices are high**, but groceries are far cheaper than eating out. One meal at an ordinary restaurant easily costs 250–350 kroner; cooking for yourself for a week can come in under 700.

blocks.title: A quick self-test
items: Write your weekly shopping list in Norwegian, with measures: *en liter melk, et grovbrød, tolv egg, et halvt kilo ost*.
Then run the whole checkout conversation on your own, out loud, from *hva koster den?* to *god helg*.
Finally: make five of your shopping sentences negative with *ingen* and *ikke noe*. *Jeg har ingen egg. Jeg trenger ikke noe brød.*

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with *noen*, *noe*, *ingen* or *ingenting*.
Fill in the blanks with the right measure.
